summary: This RFC deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option. Protocols already using it may continue to do so, but new protocols standardized in the future must not use it. It updates RFC 2711.

eli5.summary: A flag told every router "look at this packet closely." That slows things down. New protocols are told to stop using it.

questions: can new protocols use the router alert option
why is router alert a security risk
subtitle: Phasing out an IPv6 option that routers use to recognize packets needing special handling.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 Router Alert option lets routers intercept packets without examining every datagram, but it creates security risks by exposing the router's control plane to denial-of-service attacks and is rarely used beyond local networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option: existing protocols may continue to use it, but new protocols must not. This allows for gradual phase-out over time.
tldr.outcome: New protocols can be designed without relying on this option, reducing security concerns and simplifying network infrastructure. Existing deployments like MLDv2 and MRD can continue unchanged.

today: RFC 9805 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2711. It deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option for new protocols, though existing deployments will continue to use it. IANA has registered the deprecation in its official registries.

sections.title: What the IPv6 Router Alert Option Does
sections.content:
In IPv6, the Hop-by-Hop Options header can carry optional information that every router along a packet's path must examine and process. One of these options is the IPv6 Router Alert, defined in RFC 2711. It signals that a router should examine a datagram more closely, even if the datagram is not addressed to it. Without this option, routers can treat non-addressed packets as transit traffic and ignore them.

This mechanism was designed for protocols that need routers to intercept and process certain packets, such as multicast management protocols and resource reservation protocols.
sections.eli5: IPv6 lets you add special notes to packets. One note says "router, look at this closely even though it's not for you." Without it, routers ignore packets not addressed to them.

sections.title: The Security Problems
sections.content:
The Router Alert option creates several security vulnerabilities. Most significantly, RFC 6398 identifies that the option does not distinguish between legitimate router alerts and unwanted traffic. This allows attackers to flood the router's control plane with alert packets, potentially causing a denial-of-service attack.

Unlike the forwarding plane (which uses specialized hardware), the control plane typically runs on general-purpose processors and is more vulnerable to being overwhelmed. Network operators can defend against this by deploying complex access control lists, ignoring the Router Alert option, or dropping Hop-by-Hop packets at the network edge. However, as more protocols adopt the Router Alert option, these defensive measures become less effective and more computationally expensive.

Additionally, current usage of the Router Alert option appears limited to local networks. Packets with Hop-by-Hop options are frequently dropped in the Internet core, limiting the option's utility.
sections.eli5: Bad actors can send fake "look at me" messages to fool routers into wasting energy. Fixing this gets harder as more protocols use the option. And the option barely works across the whole Internet anyway.

sections.title: What Deprecation Means
sections.content:
This RFC deprecates the IPv6 Router Alert option for new protocols. Deprecation is a middle ground: it allows existing protocols that depend on the option (such as MLDv2 and MRD) to continue unchanged, but requires that new protocols standardized in the future must not use it.

Appendix A lists all protocols currently using the Router Alert option. Among these, only Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 (MLDv2) and Multicast Router Discovery (MRD) have widespread deployment. Other uses are limited, experimental, or no longer active. This narrow usage means the deprecation can take effect without breaking existing networks while preventing future protocols from introducing the same risks.
sections.eli5: The rule is: if you already use it, you can keep using it. But if you're designing a new protocol, don't use it. That way old stuff still works, but the problem stops growing.

sections.title: Future Steps
sections.content: Future work will involve developing new versions of MLDv2 and MRD that do not rely on the Router Alert option. This task is explicitly left for future RFCs and is out of scope for the current deprecation. The goal is to eventually transition even the most widely deployed users away from the option, but this requires careful coordination to avoid breaking existing multicast functionality.
sections.eli5: Someone will eventually write new versions of the main multicast tools that don't need the alert flag. But that's a separate project.

sections.title: Security and Registry Changes
sections.content:
This RFC mitigates the security considerations identified in RFC 2711, RFC 6192, and RFC 6398. IANA has marked the IPv6 Router Alert option as "DEPRECATED for New Protocols" in the destination options and hop-by-hop options registry, making the deprecation official.

Additionally, IANA closed the "IPv6 Router Alert Option Values" registry to new allocations and changed experimental codepoints to "Reserved," preventing new option values from being defined. This reinforces that the option itself is being phased out.
sections.eli5: The official registry now says "don't use this for new stuff." No new alert types can be added. This makes the deprecation official and permanent.
